subject: chemistry
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: On a Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution, adding a catalyst:
options: Changes the shape of the curve
Reduces the total number of molecules
Moves the Ea line to a lower energy, increasing the fraction of molecules with E ≥ Ea
questions.explain: A catalyst lowers Ea, so the Ea line moves left and more molecules lie beyond it; the curve itself is unchanged.

questions.q: For a titration of a strong acid with a strong base, which indicator is suitable?
questions.explain: A strong acid–strong base titration has a large vertical pH range spanning both indicators' ranges, so either works.

questions.q: At the half-neutralisation (half-equivalence) point in a weak acid–strong base titration:
questions.explain: At half-equivalence [HA] = [A⁻], so [H⁺] = Ka and pH = pKa.

questions.q: On a rate–concentration graph, an upward curve (rate ∝ [A]²) indicates:
questions.explain: A rate proportional to the square of concentration gives an upward parabola: second order.

questions.q: A catalyst increases the rate of reaction by:
options: Providing an alternative route with a lower activation energy
questions.explain: Catalysts lower Ea by offering an alternative pathway, so more molecules can react.

questions.q: In an ethanoic acid/ethanoate buffer, when a small amount of acid (H⁺) is added it is removed by reaction with:
questions.explain: Added H⁺ reacts with the conjugate base CH₃COO⁻ to form CH₃COOH, limiting the pH change.

questions.q: On a Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution, increasing temperature:
options: Shifts the peak to lower energy and makes it taller
Has no effect on the curve
Shifts the peak to higher energy and lowers it, increasing the fraction beyond Ea
questions.explain: Higher T broadens and flattens the curve, shifting the peak to higher energy with more molecules exceeding Ea.

questions.q: Which species appear in the rate equation?
options: All species in the overall equation
Only those involved up to and including the rate-determining step
questions.explain: Only reactants featuring in (or before) the rate-determining step appear in the rate equation.

questions.q: What are the units of Kc for the reaction H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g)?
questions.explain: With equal moles of gas on both sides the concentration terms cancel, so Kc is dimensionless.

questions.q: The pH of a 0.010 mol dm⁻³ solution of a strong monobasic acid (e.g. HCl) is:
questions.explain: For a fully dissociated strong acid [H⁺] = 0.010, so pH = −log(10⁻²) = 2.0.

questions.q: On a rate–concentration graph, a horizontal line indicates the reaction is:
questions.explain: Rate independent of concentration is zero order.

questions.q: For the reaction 2NO₂(g) ⇌ N₂O₄(g), increasing pressure at constant temperature shifts the equilibrium:
questions.explain: Higher pressure favours the side with fewer gas moles (1 mol N₂O₄ vs 2 mol NO₂), shifting right.

questions.q: Which combination produces a titration curve with NO sharp vertical pH jump at the equivalence point, making indicators unsuitable?
questions.explain: A weak acid–weak base titration has only a gradual pH change, so no indicator gives a sharp endpoint.

questions.q: For a first-order reaction, which is true of the half-life?
options: It decreases as the reaction proceeds
It is constant, independent of concentration
It increases as the reaction proceeds
It depends on the rate constant only at high T
questions.explain: A constant half-life is the signature of first-order kinetics.

questions.q: Heterogeneous catalysis typically involves:
options: A catalyst in the same phase, e.g. aqueous ions
A solid catalyst with gaseous/liquid reactants adsorbing onto its surface
questions.explain: Heterogeneous catalysts (e.g. solid metal) act at a surface where reactants adsorb, react, then desorb.

questions.q: What is the pH of 0.10 mol dm⁻³ NaOH at 25 °C (Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴)?
Which change alters the value of the equilibrium constant Kc for a given reaction?
options: Changing the concentration of a reactant
questions.explain: Only a change in temperature changes the value of Kc; concentration, pressure and catalysts do not.

questions.q: For a titration of a weak acid with a strong base, the most suitable indicator is:
questions.explain: The equivalence pH is above 7, in phenolphthalein's range (8.3–10), so phenolphthalein is appropriate.

questions.q: According to the Brønsted–Lowry theory, an acid is a:
questions.explain: A Brønsted–Lowry acid donates a proton (H⁺); a base accepts one.

questions.q: A buffer has [acid] = 0.10 and [salt] = 0.20 mol dm⁻³, Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵. Using [H⁺] = Ka × [acid]/[salt], pH is approximately:
For the rate equation rate = k[A]²[B], the overall order is:
questions.explain: Overall order = 2 + 1 = 3.

questions.q: For a zero-order reaction (rate = k), the units of k are:
questions.explain: Zero order: rate = k, so k has the units of rate, mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹.

questions.q: A buffer solution is one that:
options: resists changes in pH when small amounts of acid or alkali are added
questions.explain: A buffer minimises (resists) pH change on addition of small amounts of acid or base, not preventing it entirely.

questions.q: The rate constant k changes with:
questions.explain: k depends on temperature and catalysis, not on reactant concentrations.

questions.q: At 25 °C, Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ mol² dm⁻⁶. The pH of pure water is:
questions.explain: In pure water [H⁺] = [OH⁻] = √Kw = 10⁻⁷, so pH = 7.0 (neutral at 25 °C).

questions.q: Increasing concentration of a reactant increases rate because:
options: There are more particles per unit volume, so more frequent collisions
questions.explain: Higher concentration means more particles per volume and a greater collision frequency.

questions.q: If doubling [A] quadruples the rate, the order with respect to A is:
questions.explain: Rate ∝ [A]^n; 2^n = 4 gives n = 2, so second order.

questions.q: In an Arrhenius plot of ln k against 1/T, the intercept equals:
questions.explain: The y-intercept of ln k vs 1/T is ln A.

questions.q: For a first-order reaction (rate = k[A]), the units of k are:
questions.explain: For overall order 1, k has units of s⁻¹.

questions.q: A concentration–time graph that is a curve with a constant half-life indicates:
questions.explain: Constant successive half-lives identify a first-order reaction.
